opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly I don't think anyone has a fully confident answer yet. My take is that there are a couple of directions that will probably converge.

First, on the architecture side, I don't think brute-forcing vanilla full attention over a billion tokens is going to be the path. Even with all the clever kernel work and sequence parallelism, the quadratic cost, and more importantly the KV cache memory, just gets painful at that scale. So I expect some kind of hybrid: dense attention where it really matters, combined with more compressed or recurrent-style memory for the long tail. We've seen a lot of work on state space models, linear attention, sparse and local-global attention, and I think the practical answer ends up being a mix rather than one replacing the other entirely.

Second, I think the bigger, less discussed issue is actually the learning side. Even if you can technically fit a hundred million tokens in context, does the model actually *use* it well? A lot of current long-context evals are basically needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, which is a pretty low bar. Real long-context reasoning means synthesizing information spread across the whole thing, and that requires training signal that actually rewards it. Natural pretraining data mostly doesn't have dependencies at that range, so you probably need synthetic data, curricula, or RL-style objectives that explicitly force the model to integrate information over very long horizons.

And third, at some point the line between "context" and "memory" and even "weights" starts to blur. When you're talking about billions of tokens, you might be better served by something that looks more like test-time learning: the model updating some internal state or a subset of parameters as it reads, instead of holding everything verbatim. Whether we call that long context or continual learning is a bit of semantics, but I think that's where things are heading.

So my overall bet is that it's not one breakthrough architecture. It's systems plus architecture plus better training objectives, and the learning part is probably where the most interesting unsolved problems are.

r001.rationale: The response proposes updating internal state or a subset of parameters as the model reads, presenting this as test-time learning for very long contexts.

r002.rationale: It says the solution will combine architecture and systems changes with better training objectives, treating architectural and learning advances as complementary.

r003.rationale: The response does not say a new research idea must be compatible with previously developed methods.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and honestly I'm a bit skeptical of the framing of just scaling context to a billion tokens as a monolithic thing. Like, when people say "a billion token context," what they usually mean is they want the model to have access to a billion tokens of information. They don't actually mean they want quadratic attention over a billion tokens, right? That's never going to happen, and even if it did it's not clear it's what you want.

So I think the way it evolves is you have to decouple two things. One is the model's working memory, the stuff it's actively attending over, which I think stays relatively bounded, maybe a few hundred thousand to a few million tokens with good attention variants. And then there's the question of how the model accesses the rest. And I think that's where the interesting work is. Historically we had this split where retrieval was this external, kind of bolted-on thing, and long context was the "pure" approach, and there were almost like religious camps around it. I think that distinction is going to blur a lot. You'll have architectures where retrieval, or something that looks like retrieval, is a learned component inside the model rather than a separate pipeline.

The other thing is, I think the learning paradigm has to change, not just the architecture. Right now we pretrain on sequences that are, what, a few thousand tokens, and then we do some long context extension at the end and hope it generalizes. That's kind of a hack. If you actually want models to use very long contexts well, you need training signal that rewards using information from very far away, and that's actually hard to construct. Most natural data doesn't have long-range dependencies that span millions of tokens in a way that's learnable. So I suspect a lot of the progress will come from the data and objective side, like synthetic tasks or agentic setups where the model generates its own long trajectories and has to remember things it did earlier.

And then the last thing I'd say is, I've been burned enough times by efficient attention papers to be careful here. There were so many linear attention and sparse attention variants that looked great on benchmarks and then just didn't hold up at scale. So whatever ends up working for billion-token contexts, I think it'll be something that's boring and simple enough to actually survive scaling, not the most elegant mechanism on paper. It might even be a mix of things, like some state-space or recurrent component for compression plus a smaller window of full attention. I don't think there's one clean answer, which is maybe unsatisfying, but that's usually how these things go.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agentic training trajectories and remembering earlier information, but does not propose memory updated through ongoing interaction as a way to handle extremely long contexts.

r002.rationale: It says the learning paradigm has to change, “not just the architecture,” and describes changes to both training and model design.

r003.rationale: It cautions that attention methods must hold up at scale, but does not make compatibility with previously developed methods a condition for a new research idea to succeed.

astra-6.text:
I think at that scale, it becomes a question of what you actually want the model to do with the context. Having a billion tokens available and being able to reason effectively over a billion tokens are quite different things. If the task is to find one relevant passage, retrieval may be sufficient. If the answer depends on connecting information scattered across the whole context, that’s a much harder problem.

My guess is that we’ll move toward some combination of attention, retrieval, and learned memory. You probably don’t want to treat every token equally at every step. The model needs to learn what to preserve in a compressed representation, what to forget, and when to go back to the original information. And that introduces a tradeoff, because you might discard something that only becomes important much later.

So I think the learning paradigm matters as much as the architecture. Simply extending the context window doesn’t necessarily give the model a reason to use it. You need training tasks where integrating information over long distances actually helps, and where taking a shortcut through the most recent tokens doesn’t work.

I’m not sure there’s going to be one architecture that solves all of this. But I would expect the boundary between context and memory to become less clear. Instead of putting everything into one enormous forward pass, you could have a model that maintains state, accesses information selectively, and spends more computation when the question requires it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions learned memory and maintaining state, but does not say that memory is updated through ongoing interaction.

r002.rationale: It says the learning paradigm matters as much as architecture and expects both to develop to handle long contexts.

r003.rationale: It does not identify compatibility with previously developed methods as a condition for a new research idea to succeed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think at that scale, the distinction between context and learning starts to blur. If you give a model a billion tokens, are you asking it to attend to a document, or are you asking it to learn from a dataset? And should all that information live in the KV cache, or should some of it be compressed into a memory, or even into the weights through some form of test-time learning?

Architecturally, I would expect some combination of local attention, retrieval, and recurrent or compressed memory. You probably want different mechanisms for different things: preserving an exact detail is different from accumulating knowledge across millions of tokens. The challenge is deciding what to retain and making it accessible when you need it.

But I don’t think architecture alone solves this. The training objective has to reward using information over those distances. Being able to accept a billion tokens is very different from being able to do something useful with them. So I’d look at the learning paradigm and the memory architecture together, rather than just extending the context window.

r001.rationale: The response mentions compressed memory and test-time learning, but does not propose memory updated through ongoing interaction.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says to consider the learning paradigm and memory architecture together.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify compatibility with previously developed methods as a condition for a new research idea to succeed.
